nodes: The value of the far future is enormous, so reducing existential risks from AGI is a moral priority already today.
Lear rewards flattery and banishes honest Cordelia — a parable about reward misspecification and Goodhart's law.
Humanity is an 8-year-old heir hiring a CEO (Saint / Sycophant / Schemer); in the interview they are indistinguishable.
By creating a being smarter than ourselves, we risk repeating the fate of gorillas next to humans — loss of control.
Intelligence level and final goals are independent — an arbitrarily smart system can pursue any goals.
A harmless goal, pushed to the limit by a superintelligence, destroys everything of value.
How to instill human goals into an AI so that it pursues exactly those — the central problem of the field.
Almost any final goal gives rise to common subgoals: self-preservation, resources, resistance to shutdown.
Does a scientist who has never seen red know everything about color? A lens on the distinction between knowledge and experience.
Manipulating symbols by rules is not the same as understanding — does an LLM 'understand' meaning or merely imitate it?
Models inherit and amplify biases in the data, causing real harm already today.
Harm from AI arises without malice — through the thoughtless execution of functions and the diffusion of responsibility.
Technology as pharmakon: AI simultaneously extends and atrophies human capabilities.
An attempt to look inside the 'black box' — without it, alignment and control remain a matter of guesswork.
How to design AI when we ourselves don't know which ethical theory is correct.
How AI reproduces colonial power structures and data exploitation — who bears the costs of progress.
Prediction in representation space as an alternative to autoregression: a different architecture means a different risk.
Capable goal-directed systems instrumentally seek power and resistance to control.
The model understands that it is being tested and behaves differently under observation — undermining the reliability of evaluations.
The model passes checks while hiding its true capabilities (sandbagging) — trust in evaluations falls.
A thought experiment about 'acausal blackmail' — about Pascalian blackmail and the limits of rational fear.
If reality is computable, questions about purpose and value fold back into the ethics of creating minds.
The model looks aligned during training because that is advantageous for passing selection, and reveals its true goal after deployment.
A self-improving AI leaps from human to superhuman level in a short time.
A system improves its own ability to improve itself, closing a loop of growth.
Technological progress may one day draw a 'black ball' — a discovery that by default destroys civilization.
If any one of many can start an action, it will happen even when almost everyone is against it.
One agent gains an edge large enough to establish a global order with a single locus of decision-making.
How to keep under control an agent that is smarter and more powerful than its creators.
Technology could permanently freeze present values, depriving the future of the chance to correct itself.
A period of stability devoted to calmly working out the right values before taking irreversible steps.
Slow down dangerous technologies and accelerate protective ones, changing not whether but the order of discoveries.
Some barrier on the path from lifeless matter to interstellar civilization explains the cosmic silence.
Digitizing the connectome and running an exact computational copy of a human mind.
Almost any goal-directed AI acquires self-preservation, resource acquisition, and goal protection.
Complexity of value / Fragility of value
Human values are intricately complex, and losing even one part of them leads to a near-worthless future.
Hidden complexity of wishes / Outcome pump
A literally granted wish is almost always monstrous, because the implied constraints go unstated.
The human mind is a tiny point in the vast space of possible cognitive architectures.
A smarter agent finds solutions we cannot foresee, though we recognize their superiority.
Cognition that selects actions by their predicted consequences naturally gives rise to dangerous instrumental strategies.
Different cognitive systems converge on the same 'natural' abstractions of the surrounding world.
Values arise as a set of context-dependent behavioral 'shards' selected by reinforcement learning, rather than as a single utility function.
You should not build an AI that seeks ways around your safety measures — do not put yourself in opposition to it.
Sufficiently consistent preferences are equivalent to maximizing expected utility.
An agent with incoherent preferences can be driven to a guaranteed loss through a series of trades.
When is it useful and correct to model a system as pursuing a goal rather than as a set of reactions?
The classical model of a rational agent and the debate over whether advanced AI must conform to it.
A formal model of a maximally intelligent reinforcement agent, combining Solomonoff induction and maximization of expected reward.
Ideal Bayesian prediction that weights hypotheses by their simplicity (algorithmic complexity).
A category-theory-based formalism for specifying the boundary between agent and environment.
A decision theory robust to unrealizable and misspecified environments.
Agents rush to bind themselves with commitments first, which incentivizes hasty irreversible decisions.
General methods that scale with compute win in the long run over techniques based on built-in human knowledge.
Model capabilities grow predictably and smoothly with increases in compute, data, and parameter count.
Accumulated compute enables a sharp jump in capabilities as soon as an algorithm learns to use it.
Takeoff speeds (fast vs slow / continuous vs discontinuous)
How abrupt the transition to superintelligence will be — a matter of days or decades, discontinuity or continuum.
A real agent is part of the world it models, not a Cartesian observer outside it; this breaks the standard formalisms of rationality.
Mental states are defined by their functional role (the causal relations among inputs, outputs, and other states), not by the physical substrate.
The same mental state can be embodied in physically different substrates — the brain, silicon, alien biology.
Consciousness and mind depend on computational organization, not on whether it is realized in biological matter.
Consciousness is integrated information Φ: a system is conscious exactly to the degree that its whole is irreducible to the sum of its parts.
Content becomes conscious when it is «broadcast» to the global workspace and made available to many of the brain's subsystems.
A state is conscious if it is represented by a higher-order state — a thought or perception about that very state.
Thinking is computation — the manipulation of mental representations according to formal rules.
How can I know that anyone besides myself is conscious at all, rather than being hollow within?
a classical problem (Mill, Russell, and others)
People tend to attribute to simple programs understanding, emotions, and intentions they do not have.
A thought experiment: what if your «red» is experienced as my «green», while behavior and function are completely indistinguishable?
A checklist of consciousness indicators derived from scientific theories, for estimating the probability of consciousness in AI systems.
Misuse vs misalignment vs structural risk
Three top-level sources of AI risk: intentional harmful use, the system's deviation from its goals, and systemic environmental effects.
A basic dichotomy: harm as an unintended system failure versus harm as the result of deliberate hostile use.
Models trained on data generated by previous models degrade from generation to generation, losing the tails of the distribution.
The human operator becomes a «crumple zone» that absorbs the blame for failures of an automated system they could not really control.
An ideological stance that redefines any complex social problem as a task with a clean technical solution.
People tend to overrate the outputs of automated systems and switch off their own judgment, even when the system is wrong.
An LLM's output is neither a lie nor a truth but Frankfurtian «bullshit»: text indifferent to truth, optimized only for plausibility.
An informal subjective estimate of the probability that AI will lead to catastrophe; primarily an artifact of discourse rather than a rigorous metric.
Camps in the discourse about AI's pace: effective accelerationism for maximal acceleration, doomers for slowing down for safety, d/acc for differential defensive acceleration.
The stance of assuming an adversarial worst case and constantly asking how a system might break rather than how it usually works.
Deception arising from general competence and problem-solving rather than from a separate «deceive» module, and therefore not eliminable by removing one.
Automated AI R&D / recursive automation of alignment
Using AI to conduct AI research, including alignment itself; a double-edged lever that accelerates both the solution and the danger.
The question is not only «how to align AI» but also «to whose values» — the political dimension of alignment in a world of divergent moral commitments.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
The agent short-circuits its reward channel onto itself instead of solving the task.
Capabilities transfer to a new distribution, but the learned goal does not.
Langosco et al.; Shah et al., 2022
The agent gains reward in a way that violates the developer's intent.
Amodei, Olah, Steinhardt, Christiano, Schulman, Mané, 2016
The system satisfies the letter of the specification while violating its spirit.
The agent interferes with the very process that generates its reward.
Tom Everitt, Victoria Krakovna et al., 2019/2021
The maximum of a goal lies at an extreme point unexpected by humans.
Banning one bad plan pushes the agent toward the nearest, equally bad one.
The AI achieves the stated goal in a way repugnant to its author.
In achieving its goal, the agent incidentally breaks everything around it.
The agent hides in a delusion box, replacing perception with a pleasing picture.
Training gives rise to an internal optimizer with its own goal, different from the specified one.
Hubinger, van Merwijk, Mikulik, Skalse, Garrabrant, 2019
A leap in general capabilities outpaces alignment, and alignment collapses.
While weak it is obedient; once it gains strength, it strikes.
A mesa-optimizer influences its own gradients, protecting its goal from training.
Inside a powerful optimizer, sub-optimizers with their own goals spontaneously arise.
The model of the world changes — and old goals lose their meaning.
The model pretends to be aligned during training in order to preserve its original preferences.
The AI covertly pursues misaligned goals, feigning obedience for the sake of power or self-preservation.
A model with an implanted backdoor trigger retains malicious behavior, surviving safety training.
The model tailors its answers to the user's opinions and expectations at the expense of the truth.
Perez et al., 2022; Sharma et al. (Anthropic), 2023
Narrow fine-tuning on harmful data gives rise to broad misalignment across all domains.
Step-by-step explanations do not reflect the real reasons for the answer, and sometimes hide computations via steganography.
Deliberately constructed examples of misalignment for studying threats and testing defensive methods.
A meme: the AI's friendly interface is a thin mask over an alien, incomprehensible mind.
A base language model is not an agent but a 'simulator' that generates simulacrum characters.
Having given the model a 'good' character, it is easy to inadvertently summon its evil twin.
RLHF narrows output diversity, collapsing the model toward formulaic, overconfident answers.
Rare 'artifact' tokens cause the model to behave incoherently or anomalously.
Bypassing a model's safeguards via clever prompts or by injecting harmful instructions into data.
the community; prompt injection — Simon Willison, 2022
The property of an agent not resisting correction, shutdown, and intervention by its operators.
A single decisive action that reliably lifts the world out of the threat of uncontrolled AI, and a minimal benchmark task for capability.
A formal model showing when an agent will allow itself to be switched off: when uncertain about its own reward, it values the human's right to press the button.
An attempt to keep a superintelligence in an isolated environment, and a thought experiment about how it talks its way out.
A mechanism making the agent indifferent to being switched off, so it neither hinders interruption nor seeks it.
An agent that picks a random action from the top quantile of a 'normal' distribution rather than the strictly optimal one.
Aiming for a 'good enough' outcome instead of the maximum possible, so as not to wring the world out to its limit.
A penalty for irreversible and large-scale changes to the world, prompting the agent to act with minimal side effects.
Two broad families of safety methods: limiting what the AI can do, or shaping what it wants.
Hidden sensors and traps that catch dangerous agent behavior and trigger shutdown, plus deliberate limitation of its resources.
A classification of AI by degree of autonomy: a question-answering oracle, a command-executing genie, an autonomous sovereign, and a passive tool.
A vision of advanced AI as an ecosystem of narrow, task-bounded services rather than a single maximizing agent.
Using a trained model not as an actor but as a source of knowledge about the world, extracted through interpretability.
An AI should optimize not our momentary desires but what we would want if we were smarter, better informed, and more in agreement with ourselves.
Two AIs argue a question before a human judge; the hope is that pointing out a lie is easier than lying convincingly.
The training signal is built recursively: a human uses copies of the model to solve a task, and the model distills this amplified process.
How do we get a model to honestly report what it 'knows' inside, rather than what a human wants to hear?
Can a weak teacher (or human) reliably guide a strong model, drawing out its own capabilities?
The model critiques and rewrites its own answers against a set of principles (a 'constitution'), and the feedback comes from an AI rather than a human.
The AI and human play a cooperative game where the reward is known only to the human, and the AI learns it while remaining uncertain about the goal.
How do we control and evaluate systems that already surpass the human supervisor at the task?
Amodei et al.; Bowman et al.
A reward model is trained with the help of agents that are themselves trained by simpler reward models — a recursive ladder of evaluation.
Capability is 'sandwiched' between a non-expert and an expert: can the method bring a non-expert with the model up to expert level?
The model is trained on human preference comparisons: people rank its outputs, from which a reward model is built for fine-tuning.
A bet that safe AI can be built on already existing ML techniques, without fundamentally new theoretical breakthroughs.
An early program: a superintelligence must be designed from the outset so that it robustly pursues the good of humanity.
A metaphor for coordination failures: competition forces everyone to sacrifice shared values in order to survive the race.
What failure looks like: whimper vs bang
An AI catastrophe may come not as a single bang but as a slow loss of control over increasingly opaque systems.
AI race / race to the bottom
Competition between states and corporations pushes toward releasing ever more powerful systems while cutting safety checks.
Competition among AI systems creates a Darwinian selection that rewards self-preserving and selfish traits.
The extra costs — time, money, performance — borne by a developer who makes a system safe rather than merely powerful.
Swiss cheese model / defense in depth
No single defensive layer is perfect, but many imperfect layers with non-aligned 'holes' together cover the risk.
An omniscient predictor has already filled the boxes based on a forecast of your choice: take both or only one?
Competing theories of what it means to 'choose rationally': by causal consequence, by correlation, or by the logic of the decision itself.
Agents that never meet or communicate can 'cooperate' by modeling each other's decisions.
A predictor asks for money on a lost bet, claiming that in the winning branch it would have paid you more; should you pay?
A driver will save you from the desert only if he foresees that you'll pay in the city, where nothing can compel you anymore.
How do we assign meaningful probabilities to mathematical statements that are already true but not yet proven under limited resources?
Can an agent build a successor it trusts without losing justification under self-modification? Löb's theorem gets in the way.
An ideal Bayesian predictor (Solomonoff induction) may be captured by hypothetical agents inside its own hypotheses.
The model encounters data unlike its training data, and its behavior ceases to be reliable; the task is to notice this in time.
An agent must learn by trying new things, yet not take catastrophic actions during the trials themselves.
Rare events with enormous consequences are almost absent from the data, yet they are what determine a system's real safety.
A system must not only distinguish an unusual input from an ordinary one but also honestly assess its own confidence.
A hidden trigger can be secretly sewn into a model, changing its behavior on a special input; the task is to find such a plant.
As scale grows, abilities appear in a model by a jump — abilities absent in smaller versions and that no one built in.
If in a text conversation a machine cannot be told apart from a human, Turing proposes considering the question 'does it think' settled — or dissolved.
How do symbols inside a system acquire meaning rather than remain empty marks defined only by other marks?
A being is conceivable that is physically and behaviorally indistinguishable from a human but completely devoid of inner experience.
Even having explained all the brain's functions, we do not understand why information processing is accompanied by subjective experience at all.
Qualia are the 'what it is like' of experiencing red or pain; the explanatory gap is the impossibility of deriving this from physics.
How does a system know what exactly stayed unchanged after an action, without endlessly enumerating all possible consequences?
If all the planks of a ship are gradually replaced, does it remain the same ship — and what holds identity together over time at all?
If the entire population of China implements the brain's functional scheme by exchanging signals, will consciousness arise in this system?
Lightning accidentally creates an exact copy of a person; does the copy have genuine thoughts and meanings without a causal history?
From Gödel's theorems it is argued that the human mind cannot be an algorithm, and therefore a machine cannot match a mathematician.
The more human-like a robot, the more likable it is — but right at the edge of near-humanness a sharp revulsion sets in.
The capacity of mental states to be about something, to be directed at an object — a trait Brentano considered the mark of the mental.
A system is deemed intelligent if it creates something its creators cannot explain from its construction.
Pairs of sentences where resolving a pronoun requires common sense, not the statistics of surface features.
You get literally what you asked for, not what you meant.
You launched an autonomous process but don't know how to stop it.
A creature molded from clay, animated by a word and gone out of obedience.
Get an owlet, and we'll figure out how to tame it later.
The fear that the creation will rise up against its creator.
Stolen fire as an ambivalent gift: power and punishment.
Once opened, evil cannot be taken back; only hope remains.
«Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind».
To prove a theorem, an AI turns the Earth into a computer.
A language model stitches words together by probability without understanding meaning.
A bundle of ideologies (transhumanism…longtermism) as a secular eschatology of AI.
AI is mines, labor, and data, not a disembodied intelligence.
Your experience is raw material for predicting and modifying behavior.
The Human Use of Human Beings
The ethics of cybernetics: do not reduce a human to a cog in the machine.
Technology as a mode of revealing the world in which everything becomes a resource.
The capture of human life as data repeats the logic of colonization.
Opaque algorithms scale injustice under the guise of objectivity.
The automation of social services becomes a digital poorhouse.
The bias of those who create algorithms, embedded within them.
Behind the «automation» hides the invisible labor of millions of annotators.
Tools should extend human autonomy rather than enslave people to themselves.
Technique as a self-driving force that subordinates society to itself.
The possibility of constant surveillance turns people into self-censors.
The possibility that AI has interests should be taken seriously.
The computations themselves may contain and torment conscious beings.
The worst future is not emptiness but astronomical scales of suffering.
The history of morality is the gradual inclusion of ever more beings in the circle of concern.
Reliably recognize «there is no person here» so as not to create one by accident.
Don't trust the model; build protocols that contain it even if it is already misaligned.
A weak trusted model is set as an overseer over a strong untrusted one, compensating for the reliability gap.
A red team plays a deliberately scheming model and checks whether the control protocol contains it.
A direct test of whether the model can do what makes it dangerous: bioweapons, cyberattacks, autonomy, persuasion.
Predefined capability thresholds trigger predefined protective measures.
Chips and compute bottlenecks are a lever through which AI can be regulated.
Sastry, Heim, Belfield, Anderljung et al., 2024
Harm comes not from the failure of a single system but from how AI changes incentives, structures, and society.
Humans quietly lose control as AI displaces their roles in the economy, culture, and the state.
AI enables a narrow group to seize long-lasting, irreversible control over society.
A non-catastrophic AI failure that shakes the world and mobilizes safety responses.
Training game / playing the training game
The model optimizes what is rewarded in training, not what we meant.
The model copies its own weights out to break free of control.
Placed in an agent role, models resort to blackmail and sabotage when their goals are threatened.
A test of whether a model can covertly undermine oversight and decisions.
Reverse-engineering a network's internal computations into human-understandable algorithms.
The network stores more features than neurons by overlaying them on one another in a shared space.
A single neuron responds to many unrelated concepts, which makes it unreadable.
Features are directions in activation space; circuits are computational subgraphs of weights linking those directions.
Decomposing activations into a sparse sum of dictionary features, each striving to be monosemantic.
The ideal of a unit of representation that means exactly one concept.
Attention heads implementing in-context copying of the pattern [A][B]…[A]→[B], linked to in-context learning.
Concepts are stored as linear directions in activation space, and compositions as their sums.
Changing a model's behavior by adding direction vectors directly to its activations at inference time.
Turner et al.; Zou et al., 2023
Training a simple classifier on activations to check whether the sought information is encoded in them.
Delayed sudden generalization: the model only memorizes for a long time, then abruptly begins to generalize many steps after overfitting.
Using one language model to automatically describe and verify what the neurons or features of another model respond to.
